name: The Fox and the Complete Tree Traversal
description: The fox Yae climbed the tree of the Sacred Sakura. A tree is a connected undirected graph that does not contain cycles. The fox uses her magical powers to move around the tree. Yae can jump from vertex $$$v$$$ to another vertex $$$u$$$ if and only if the distance between these vertices does not exceed $$$2$$$. In other words, in one jump Yae can jump from vertex $$$v$$$ to vertex $$$u$$$ if vertices $$$v$$$ and $$$u$$$ are connected by an edge, or if there exists such vertex $$$w$$$ that vertices $$$v$$$ and $$$w$$$ are connected by an edge, and also vertices $$$u$$$ and $$$w$$$ are connected by an edge. After Yae was able to get the sakura petal, she wondered if there was a cyclic route in the tree $$$v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$$$ such that: the fox can jump from vertex $$$v_i$$$ to vertex $$$v_{i + 1}$$$, the fox can jump from vertex $$$v_n$$$ to vertex $$$v_1$$$, all $$$v_i$$$ are pairwise distinct. Help the fox determine if the required traversal exists.
input_specification: The first line contains one integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) —the number of vertices of the tree. Each of the following $$$n - 1$$$ lines contains two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n$$$, $$$u \ne v$$$) — vertices connected by an edge. It is guaranteed that these edges form a tree.
output_specification: On the first line, print " Yes " (without quotes) if the required route of the tree exists, or " No " (without quotes) otherwise. If the required tree traversal exists, on the second line print $$$n$$$ integers of different integers $$$v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$$$ ($$$1 \le v_i \le n$$$) — the vertices of the tree in traversal order. If there are several correct traversals, output any of them.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1819C — The Fox and the Complete Tree Traversal [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
